declarations.documentation:
Get a usable Google access token, served by `provider` for the extent of a continuation — the
capability the tools require (`with … credential`). Each ask resolves the provider's named
credential through the runtime (`oauth.token`): the runtime returns the stored token while its recorded
lifetime holds and refreshes it against the stored token endpoint once due, so no token bookkeeping
lives in the program. The token is a `string of private` — it flows only toward a submission sink (the
`Bearer` header). A credential that needs a human (never authorized, or refresh-dead) never throws: the
ask PARKS the run on a `prelude.oauth.authorize` escalation and resumes once the browser flow completes.
A transient resolution failure throws `oauth.server_error` at the provider.

credentials-unification shape: `use google_calendar.provider(source = credentials.oauth(name =

cache and its refresh, so this provider holds no secret and keeps no state); an unauthorized oauth
credential parks the run on a `prelude.oauth.authorize` escalation rather than failing, and a
transient resolution failure throws at the asking call.

anyOf.description:
api_error: An authenticated API call failed for anything OTHER than the credential: a non-2xx @status@ that is not
401/403 — a malformed request, a resource that is not there, a rate limit, a server error. Nothing about
the caller's identity is in question, so backing off and replaying the call AS IT STANDS is the whole
recovery for the transient half, and the other half (a 400 the service is simply refusing) will keep
failing until the ARGUMENT changes.

WHICH half a given failure is, is read off @status@ and nowhere else: 408 / 429 / 5xx are the transient
ones a retry policy should back off and repeat, every other status is a refusal that will repeat forever.
That is the whole reason the status RIDES on the error instead of being folded into a sentence — a retry
policy downstream reads a number, never a message.

@context@ says WHICH call failed in the caller's own words; @message@ carries the server's own body
verbatim, because it is the diagnosis and a model handed this error reads it and adjusts.

anyOf.description:
auth_error: An authenticated API call was rejected over WHO IS CALLING: the endpoint answered @status@ — 401 or
403 — so the CREDENTIAL is what failed: revoked, expired past what its holder believed, or scoped too
narrowly for this call. Retrying with the SAME credential cannot succeed; the recovery is a fresh
RESOLUTION of it, which is why the ordinary composition is a `replay` converter that signals
`replay.interrupted`: the re-run resolves the credential again, and one the runtime cannot refresh parks
the run on a `prelude.oauth.authorize` escalation — a human's re-authorization prompt — rather than
failing. That is the whole line this variant draws: an `auth_error` may need a HUMAN before any retry can
work, an `api_error` never does.

(403 is read as auth even though some APIs also spend it on quota exhaustion. The access-rejection reading
is the one worth composing a re-resolution around, and a quota 403 that is replayed simply fails again.)

declarations.documentation:

the user's own, or an address like "team@example.com"); @time_min@ / @time_max@ bound the window as
RFC3339 timestamps (e.g. "2026-07-11T00:00:00Z"); @max_results@ caps how many come back. Returns the
events trimmed to id / summary / start / end / link — small enough to feed straight back to the model.

A RECURRING event is returned EXPANDED into its individual occurrences, each with its own id and its own
start: a weekly meeting crossing the window is several `event`s here, not one rule to interpret. So
nothing about listing, or about `watch`, needs to know that recurrence exists. An occurrence's id
addresses that one occurrence (`update_event` / `delete_event` on it affects only it), which is NOT the
series-master id `create_event` returned.

declarations.documentation:
Tool: query a calendar's FREE/BUSY over a window — the purpose-built way to find an opening, instead of
listing every event and reasoning over the gaps. @calendar_id@ is the calendar ("primary" for the user's
own); @time_min@ / @time_max@ bound the window as RFC3339 timestamps (e.g. "2026-07-11T00:00:00Z").
Returns the BUSY windows only — each a `{ start, end }` merged across whatever events overlap it, with no
title or detail — so the openings are the gaps BETWEEN them (and before the first and after the last,
within the window). Google caps a free/busy query at a window of a few months; a wider one comes back as an
`http.api_error` carrying Google's own message.

declarations.checkedType: agent(calendar_id: string, description?: string, end: string, recurrence?: array[string], start: string, summary: string, time_zone?: string) -> event with credential | throw[api_error | auth_error | fetch_error | parse_error] | io
declarations.documentation:
Tool: create an event on a calendar — one event, or a whole RECURRING SERIES in a single call when
@recurrence@ is given. @calendar_id@ is the target calendar ("primary" for the user's own); @summary@ is
the title; @start@ / @end@ are RFC3339 timestamps (e.g. "2026-07-11T15:00:00+09:00") and, for a
recurring event, describe its FIRST occurrence — the rule repeats that occurrence rather than adding
occurrences of its own; @description@ is optional detail.

@recurrence@ holds RFC 5545 recurrence rules, passed to Google verbatim (Google validates them; a
malformed rule comes back as an `http.api_error`). Almost always ONE "RRULE:..." string — which is how a
standing appointment is registered once instead of an event per occurrence:

  - every Wednesday and Sunday, up to and including 2026-08-31:
    ["RRULE:FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=WE,SU;UNTIL=20260831T000000Z"]
  - every weekday for the next 10 occurrences: ["RRULE:FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=MO,TU,WE,TH,FR;COUNT=10"]
  - the same day of every month, with no end: ["RRULE:FREQ=MONTHLY"]

A series ends by `UNTIL` (a COMPACT UTC timestamp — `YYYYMMDDTHHMMSSZ`, no dashes or colons, unlike
@start@ / @end@ — and inclusive) or by `COUNT` (a number of occurrences); give one or neither, never
both. Omit both for a series that runs forever. Weekdays are the two-letter `MO TU WE TH FR SA SU`.

@time_zone@ is an IANA zone name ("Asia/Tokyo", "America/New_York") and is REQUIRED whenever
@recurrence@ is given: Google expands the rule in that zone, so "every Wednesday at 10:00" has to know
whose 10:00, and it is what keeps an occurrence at 10:00 local across a daylight-saving shift. A
recurring event without it is rejected as an `http.api_error` (a 400). It applies to both @start@ and @end@,
and is unnecessary for a single event — an RFC3339 offset already fixes one instant.

Returns the created event. For a recurring one that is the SERIES MASTER: its start / end are the first
occurrence's, and its id addresses the WHOLE series (`update_event` on it changes every occurrence,
`delete_event` on it removes them all). To see the individual occurrences, list the window with
`list_events`, which expands them.

declarations.checkedType: agent(calendar_id: string, description?: string, end?: string, event_id: string, start?: string, summary?: string) -> event with credential | throw[api_error | auth_error | fetch_error | parse_error] | io
declarations.documentation:
Tool: update an existing event on a calendar. @calendar_id@ is the calendar ("primary" for the
user's own) and @event_id@ the event's id (from `list_events` / `create_event`). Only the fields you pass
are changed — @summary@ (title), @start@ / @end@ (RFC3339 timestamps, e.g. "2026-07-11T15:00:00Z") and
@description@ each default to `null`, and a `null` field is LEFT EXACTLY AS IT IS. Returns the updated
event (its id and the link to open it).

PASSING `""` IS A DIFFERENT INSTRUCTION FROM OMITTING: it EMPTIES the field. That is how an event's
@description@ or @summary@ is cleared — the one operation this tool could not express while an empty
string meant "not given". @start@ and @end@ have no empty form (an event must have both), so pass a
timestamp or leave them alone; an empty one is a 400 from Google.

WHICH id you pass decides the REACH on a recurring event, and Google draws that line, not this package.
The series-master id (what `create_event` returned for a recurrence) edits EVERY occurrence at once; a
single occurrence's id (what `list_events` returns) edits only that one, and Google records it as an
exception to the series. There is no third mode here — "this and all following" is not something this
tool expresses. The recurrence RULE itself is not patchable through this agent: to change a series'
schedule or its end date, `delete_event` the master and `create_event` a new series.

declarations.documentation:
Tool: delete an event from a calendar. @calendar_id@ is the calendar ("primary" for the user's
own) and @event_id@ the event's id (from `list_events` / `create_event`). Returns null; deleting an

declarations.checkedType: agent(calendar_id: string, cursor_at: fresh | resume, deliver_to: agent(value: event) -> null with E2, lead_time_milliseconds: number, poll_interval_milliseconds: number) -> never with credential | throw[watch_misconfigured | api_error | auth_error | fetch_error | parse_error] | get | set | E2 | io
declarations.documentation:
Watch a calendar for upcoming TIMED events and deliver each one to @deliver_to@ as it enters the lead
window — `poll.subscribe` under a Calendar adapter, so it composes under `parallel [ … ]` beside any other
daemon and never resolves (`-> never`). Every @poll_interval_milliseconds@ it lists the events whose START
lies within @lead_time_milliseconds@ ahead of the tick and delivers each one not seen before. All-day
events are NOT covered (they have no instant to place in the lead window); this watch is for timed events
only. @deliver_to@'s effects @E@ flow to the caller's handlers unchanged.

DELIVERY IS AT-LEAST-ONCE — `poll.subscribe`'s contract, in its words. An event reaches @deliver_to@ one or
more times, never zero: the commit lands only after a delivery returns, so a crash or a throw in between
re-delivers exactly that event on the next tick. EXACTLY-ONCE IS BUILT AT THE DESTINATION, by making the
delivery idempotent — key it on the (id, start) pair this subscription dedups by, which is stable for an
occurrence that has not moved.

THE DEDUP KEY IS `id ++ " " ++ start`, and the memory is the last 200 of them (`poll.seen_set`) rather
than a cursor: a calendar has no receive clock to advance one along, because what this reports is a
TRANSITION into the window and an event created minutes before it starts enters the window without ever
having been "new" in arrival order. So an event whose start has not moved is delivered once, and an event
whose start MOVED is a different key and re-notifies — which is the right answer for a rescheduled meeting.
200 is far above what one lead window holds; a calendar that delivered 200 events while one was still
inside its own window could re-notify that one.

THE EVENTS ALREADY INSIDE THE LEAD WINDOW WHEN THE SUBSCRIPTION FIRST STARTS ARE NOT DELIVERED. The first
tick only RECORDS them (`poll.skip_backlog` under a seen-set is a priming tick): a watch started twenty
minutes before a meeting, with a thirty-minute lead, says nothing about that meeting — what it reports is
an event ENTERING the window from then on. A watch is a subscription to a transition, not a report of the
current state; `list_events` answers "what is coming up".

@cursor_at@ DECIDES WHAT A RESTART DOES. `poll.resume(key = ...)` keeps the memory in the store, so a
runtime restart, a re-forked fiber and a `replay` re-run all come back holding the keys they already
delivered — which is what stops the re-notification storm a re-primed memory would cause. `poll.fresh()`
re-primes instead: the activation is silent about the window it lands in and reports the entries after it.
NEITHER BACKFILLS. A seen-set subscription has no floor to list from, so whatever crossed the window while
the watch was down is gone either way; `resume` buys quiet, not recovery. There is no default — a watch
that will be re-forked wants `resume` with a key of its own, and a second watch sharing one key overwrites
the first's memory.

RECURRING events need nothing special: the listing expands them into one entry per occurrence, each with
its own id and start, so a weekly meeting is delivered once per week and the dedup is per occurrence rather
than per series.

@poll_interval_milliseconds@ must not exceed @lead_time_milliseconds@ — a wider interval leaves the gap
(T+lead, T+poll) covered by no window, silently dropping events that start there. That is a program
defect, rejected at entry with `watch_misconfigured` (a `panic` in spirit; a Katari program cannot raise
one).

No retry is built in — a poll failure (an http error, a rejected token, a @deliver_to@ that throws)
propagates and kills the subscription, exactly as an uncaught failure in any callee does. Compose
resilience by wrapping the watch in a replay provider (`replay.forever` with a converter that replays the
transient blips AND `http.auth_error` — the re-run re-resolves the token, and a credential needing a human
parks on the runtime's authorize escalation rather than failing). The first poll is one
@poll_interval_milliseconds@ in (a `time.watch` occurrence fires one interval after the start), and that
first poll is the priming one, so the earliest notification a watch can produce is two intervals after it
starts.

effects.rendered: E | io | credential | store.get | store.set | prelude.throw[watch_misconfigured | http.api_failure | http.fetch_error | json.parse_error]

declarations.checkedType: agent(calendar_id: string, lead: number, window_start: number) -> array[event] with credential | throw[api_error | auth_error | fetch_error | parse_error] | io
declarations.documentation:
List every timed event whose START lies in the window [@window_start@, @window_start@ + @lead@),
across ALL result pages — `watch`'s per-poll listing. Paginates on `nextPageToken` so a busy window is
delivered in full rather than truncated at one page. The recursion depth is the number of pages in one
poll (small and bounded — a single lead window rarely spans more than a page), not the daemon's
lifetime, so it does not accumulate like a per-tick loop would. Internal to `watch`.

declarations.documentation:
One Calendar event object as an `event`. Google nests the moment under `start` / `end` as either a
`dateTime` (timed) or a `date` (all-day); `read_moment` classifies it and `moment_text` renders the
string the model reads.
